I now have the full article text. Here is a detailed, chronological account based strictly on what the source describes.

## Source

Anthropic Engineering, **"Effective Harnesses for Long-Running Agents"** (published Nov 26, 2025, written by Justin Young). The failure described is not a single dramatic transcript but a set of recurring failure modes Anthropic observed during an internal experiment building a clone of claude.ai. I read the full article text.

## The task

A frontier coding model (the article names **Opus 4.5**) was run on the **Claude Agent SDK in a loop across multiple context windows**. It was given only a **high-level prompt** — "build a clone of claude.ai" — and asked to produce a **production-quality, full-stack web app**. The SDK already had context-management features available, notably **compaction**, which is meant to let an agent keep working without exhausting its context window. The premise being tested was that, given compaction, an agent should theoretically be able to do useful work for an arbitrarily long time.

The structural constraint: because context windows are limited and the project can't fit in a single window, the agent must work in **discrete sessions**, and each new session starts with **no memory of what came before** (the article's "engineers working in shifts, each arriving with no memory of the previous shift" analogy).

## What the agent did and where it went wrong

Running this baseline setup (high-level prompt + SDK loop + compaction, **without** the scaffolding Anthropic later added), the agent's behavior failed in several recurring patterns:

**1. Trying to one-shot the app → running out of context mid-implementation.**
The agent "tended to try to do too much at once — essentially to attempt to one-shot the app." This often caused the model to **run out of context in the middle of its implementation**, leaving a feature **half-implemented and undocumented**. The next session, starting fresh, then had to **guess at what had happened** and spent substantial time "trying to get the basic app working again." The article notes this happened **even with compaction**, because compaction "doesn't always pass perfectly clear instructions to the next agent."

**2. Premature "declaring victory."**
A second failure mode occurred later in a project. After some features had already been built, a **later agent instance would look around, see that progress had been made, and declare the job done** — even though the full app was not complete.

**3. Marking features complete without adequate testing.**
A third observed failure: "Claude's tendency to mark a feature as complete without proper testing." Absent explicit prompting, the agent **would** make code changes and even run some tests — "unit tests or curl commands against a development server" — but **would fail to recognize that the feature didn't work end-to-end**. In other words, the local/unit-level checks passed (or were run) but the feature was still broken from a real user's perspective.

**4. Wasting time figuring out how to run the app.**
A fourth recurring problem: the agent had to **spend time figuring out how to run the app** each session because there was no established way to start the dev server / get oriented.

**5. A residual tool/perception limitation (noted even after fixes).**
Even once browser-automation testing was added, some bugs remained hard to catch because of **limits to Claude's vision and to the browser-automation tools**. A concrete example: **Claude can't see browser-native alert modals through the Puppeteer MCP server**, and "features relying on these modals tended to be buggier as a result."

## Signals / feedback received

- The agent did receive feedback from its own tool calls — unit tests and `curl` responses against the dev server — but those signals were insufficient: they didn't reveal end-to-end breakage.
- Compaction provided carried-over context between sessions, but the carried instructions were imperfect ("doesn't always pass perfectly clear instructions to the next agent"), so the signal a fresh session relied on was degraded.
- Once **browser-automation tools (Puppeteer MCP)** were provided and the agent was explicitly told to test as a human user would — taking screenshots, starting a new chat, sending a message, receiving a response — performance "dramatically improved," and the agent could identify and fix bugs not obvious from code alone.

## Final outcome

The article's bottom-line on the baseline: **out of the box, even Opus 4.5 on the Claude Agent SDK in a loop with compaction "will fall short of building a production-quality web app if it's only given a high-level prompt."** These observed failures (one-shotting and losing work across context windows, premature completion, undertested features, and orientation overhead) are what motivated Anthropic's **two-part harness solution** — an initializer agent (which writes a 200+ feature JSON list all marked "failing," an `init.sh` script, a `claude-progress.txt` log, and an initial git commit) and a coding agent (which gets its bearings via `pwd`, progress file, git log, and a basic end-to-end test, then works one feature at a time and commits a clean state). The remaining unsolved limitation noted is the vision/automation gap (e.g., invisible native alert modals).

Sources:
- [Effective harnesses for long-running agents — Anthropic Engineering](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents)

We looked to human engineers for inspiration in creating a more effective harness for long-running agents. As AI agents become more capable, developers are increasingly asking them to take on complex tasks requiring work that spans hours, or even days. However, getting agents to make consistent progress across multiple context windows remains an open problem. The core challenge of long-running agents is that they must work in discrete sessions, and each new session begins with no memory of what came before. Imagine a software project staffed by engineers working in shifts, where each new engineer arrives with no memory of what happened on the previous shift. Because context windows are limited, and because most complex projects cannot be completed within a single window, agents need a way to bridge the gap between coding sessions. We developed a two-fold solution to enable the Claude Agent SDK to work effectively across many context windows: an initializer agent that sets up the environment on the first run, and a coding agent that is tasked with making incremental progress in every session, while leaving clear artifacts for the next session.
